canonicalExplanation.summary: When a form is submitted, the browser collects every **enabled control that has a `name`**, pairs it with its value (`q=html+tables`) and sends it to the form's `action` URL using its `method`. **GET** puts the pairs in the URL — great for searches you can bookmark or share. **POST** sends them in the request body — use it for anything that changes data or includes private values. A control without a name is simply not sent.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
You search a course site for "html tables", like the results, and copy the URL to a friend. It works — because the search form used GET and put your query in the address. But a login form using GET would put your password in the address bar, the history and server logs! A search form uses GET so its named query appears in a bookmarkable URL. In this lesson you'll build and explain a form's serialized submission without exposing sensitive values in a query URL.

```predict
{"question": "`<input type=\"text\" value=\"Asha\">` (no name) sits inside a form. Is it submitted?", "options": ["Yes, all visible inputs are sent", "No — controls without a name aren't submitted"], "answer": 1, "why": "The name is the key in each key=value pair. No name, no pair."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Paragraph and inline meaning** and **Relative and absolute URLs** — action is a URL.

sections.heading: The model: named controls → key=value pairs → action + method
sections.body:
```html
<form action="/search" method="get" role="search">
  <label for="q">Search courses</label>
  <input id="q" name="q" type="search">
  <button>Search</button>
</form>
```

Typing `html tables` and submitting sends: **GET /search?q=html+tables**

| Attribute | Decides |
|---|---|
| `action`. | where the data goes. |
| `method="get"`. | data in the URL — for reading/searching. |
| `method="post"`. | data in the body — for changes and private data. |
| `name` on each control. | the key in the submitted pair. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Is POST data encrypted or secret?", "answer": "No. POST keeps data out of the URL, history and many logs, but only HTTPS encrypts it in transit. Always use HTTPS for private data."}
```

sections.heading: Choose the method

includes: Explain how named controls are serialized and sent to action with a method.
Choose GET for searches and POST for changes or private data.
excludes: File uploads and multipart encoding in depth.

outcomes: Build and explain a form's serialized submission without exposing sensitive values in a query URL.

examples.title: A bookmarkable search
examples.situation: A search form uses GET so its named query appears in a bookmarkable URL.
walkthrough: **Named query:** the input has `name="q"`, so its value becomes the q pair.
**Bookmarkable URL:** the results page can be bookmarked, shared and re-run by the browser.
examples.result: The search results live at a URL that works for anyone who opens it.

examples.title: The password in the address bar
examples.situation: A login form has `method="get"`. After signing in, the URL shows `/login?user=asha&pass=S3cret!`.
walkthrough: GET serialized the password into the query string.
It's now in browser history, the server's access logs and possibly analytics.
Fix: `method="post"` over HTTPS, and ask users to change the exposed password.
examples.result: Credentials no longer appear in URLs, history or logs.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The form element automatically sends every visible control, even when it lacks a name.
misconceptions.correction: Only enabled controls with a name attribute are submitted, as name=value pairs. Visibility doesn't matter; the name does.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why wasn't Asha's value sent?

analogy.example: Submitting a form is like **filling in a courier slip**: each labelled box (name) gets a value, and the slip goes to an address (action). GET writes everything on the outside of the envelope; POST puts it inside.
usefulFor: seeing GET as "visible on the envelope"
limitations: Envelopes can still be opened; only HTTPS seals the data in transit.
An unlabelled box is thrown away — like an unnamed control.

steps.explanation: The form collects the named query control and its value.
Using GET, the pair is encoded into the URL.
The search form's named query appears in a bookmarkable URL.

trace.textAlternative: Submitting a GET search form. Step 1, Collect: q is html tables. The form collects the named query control and its value. Step 2, Serialize: query string is q=html+tables. Using GET, the pair is encoded into the URL. Step 3, Result: URL is /search?q=html+tables; bookmarkable is yes. The search form's named query appears in a bookmarkable URL.

faded.prompt: For "A bookmarkable search", explain how the search form uses GET so its named query appears in a bookmarkable URL, including the exact URL for "html tables".
expectedEvidence: Names the example "A bookmarkable search": a search form uses GET.
Its named query q is serialized.
It appears in a bookmarkable URL: /search?q=html+tables.
The search results live at a URL that works for anyone who opens it; private data would use POST instead.

nearTransfer.prompt: A feedback form has fields name, email and message and saves to a database. Write the form tag with the right method and explain which fields will be sent.
expectedEvidence: All three fields sent because each has a name.

farTransfer.prompt: Build a filter form (category select + price range) that uses GET. Submit it, bookmark the URL, and explain how the server could read each value.
scaffold: Look at the URL after submitting.
expectedEvidence: Working GET form producing a readable query string.

remediation.explanation: Before submitting, list each control's **name = value**. Anything without a name disappears. Then ask: **does this read or change data? Any secrets?** Read + no secrets → GET; otherwise → POST.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The password in the address bar".

recap.summary: To build and explain a form's serialized submission, give each control a name, set action and method, and remember only named, enabled controls are sent. Use GET for bookmarkable searches and POST for changes or sensitive values — never expose secrets in a query URL.
retrievalPrompts: Where does GET put the data?
